newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia sex industry claims moral victory.
newsitem.headline: Australia sex industry claims moral victory.

text.p: Australia's sex industry claimed a victory against moral conservatism on Thursday after it finally secured a venue courageous enough to stage the nation's first "Sexpo".

Speaking at the opening of the inaugural health, sexuality and lifestyle exhibition in the usually staid city of Melbourne, organisers said several venues declined to stage the event before a large hotel here finally accepted.

"They refused the booking when they found out the content of the show," organiser David Ross told assembled sex industry workers and reporters as exhibitors from adult movie houses and sex aid merchants began to peddle their wares.
"We have no intention of offending anyone -- it's simply an attempt to inform the public about the adult industry," said Ross, president of Melbourne's Adult Entertainment Association.
Sexpo is guarded by a big warning sign prohibiting entry to people aged under 18 and aims to distribute "frank and accurate information on all matters sexual".
Its first visitors were middle-aged women attending a plant-breeders' conference in the same hotel. "They asked for a couple of free tickets (to visit again)," Ross said.
Organisers expect up to 20,000 people to visit Sexpo over the next four days. For A$20 (US$15.80), each of them can take away a "show bag" full of erotica.
"We have gone about producing a show that will inform the public in a non-threatening, almost clinical environment...," Ross told Reuters.
"The fact that it's an exhibition and the first of its kind, it gives us credibility."

Sexpo's dozens of exhibitors include mainstream bodies like the Victoria state Aids Council and pay-television operator Australis Media Ltd, which recently launched the country's first adult movie channel.
Adult-rated sites on the Internet worldwide computer network are also promoted, with visitors invited to "Ride the Net".
Industry lobby group the Eros Foundation estimates the sex industry rings up around A$200 million in sales in Australia each year and says the market is growing.
Eros Foundation president Fiona Patten said the exhibition proved the industry had come of age in Australia.
"We are no longer this raincoat brigade and dark, dingy sort of business -- if indeed we ever were," she said at the opening.
